questions.question: What are the main purpose of first aid? (U) CO 1
questions.solution_html:
• First aid is the immediate assistance given to a person who is ill or injured. The main purpose of
  • first aid is to provide timely and effective assistance to individuals in emergencies. This involves
  • preserving life, preventing further injury or illness, and promoting recovery until more advanced
  • medical care is available.

questions.question: What is the difference between adult and child CPR. (U) CO 2
questions.solution_html:
• The main difference between adult and child CPR lies in the technique and sequence of actions.
  • For a child, use one of your hands. Place the heel of the hand at their sternum, which is in the
  • center of the chest, between and slightly below their nipples. Press down hard and fast around 1.5
  • inches deep, or one-third the depth of the chest. For an infant, use two fingers. Place your fingers
  • in the center of their chest, between and slightly below the nipples. For adults, place the heel of
  • one hand in the middle of the chest. Place your other hand on top of the first hand and interlace
  • the fingers. For adults, compress the chest to a depth of at least 2 inches. Rescue breaths follow
  • the same ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths for both adults and children

questions.question: What should you do if someone is in a drowning incident? (U) CO 2
questions.solution_html:
• Move the person out of the water. Check the level of response, open the airway and check
  • breathing. If the casualty is unresponsive and not breathing normally shout for help and
  • immediately star CPR. Give five initial rescue breaths, follow this with 30 chest compressions,
  • then two rescue breaths. Repeat the procedure till casualty shows signs of becoming responsive
  • or until help arrives.

questions.question: Why should the bleeding injury elevate above the heart level? (K) CO 5
questions.solution_html:
• Elevating a bleeding injury above heart level is a first-aid technique used to help control bleeding.
  • By elevating the injured area above the heart, gravity reduces the blood pressure in the blood
  • vessels at the injury site, making it harder for blood to flow out of the wound. This reduces the
  • stress on the heart. Slower blood flow allows the natural clotting. Elevation also helps to reduce
  • swelling in the injured area.

  • casualty.

questions.question: Explain the RICE method. (U) CO
questions.solution_html:

  • following a strain, sprain, or other similar injury can help more quickly recover and get back to

  • Ice : Apply ice or a cold pack to the area for 20 minutes at a time every 4 hours
  • Compression : Wrap the area with a bandage to reduce swelling and provide support
  • Elevation : Keep the injured area raised above the level of the heart

questions.question: What is the difference between voluntary and involuntary muscles? (K) CO 2
questions.solution_html:
• Muscles in the human body can be classified into voluntary and involuntary muscles based on
  • whether their movement is under conscious control. Voluntary muscles are under our conscious
  • control and are responsible for body movements like walking, lifting, and running. Skeletal
  • Muscles are voluntary muscles and striated in appearance due to organized muscle fibers.
  • Involuntary muscles are not under our conscious control and contract and relax automatically.
  • They are also known as unstriated or smooth muscles. Smooth Muscles are found in the walls of
  • internal organs (e.g., stomach, intestines, and blood vessels). Cardiac Muscles are found only in
  • the heart. Involuntary, works automatically to maintain the heartbeat.

questions.question: Describe the first aid protocol and its significance in the initial assessment of a casualty. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the first aid protocol and its significance in the initial assessment of a
  • casualty.
  • Answer: The first aid protocol begins with the steps of DRABC – Danger, Response,
  • Airway, Breathing and Circulation . First, the first aider checks for any danger to ensure
  • the scene is safe. Next, the casualty is checked for respo nse to understand their condition.
  • Then the airway is opened, and breathing is checked to see if the person is getting enough
  • oxygen. Finally, circulation is assessed by looking for movement or signs of severe
  • bleeding. This protocol is important because i t helps the first aider act quickly, identify
  • life-threatening problems, and give the right care without wasting time. It guides the
  • helper to stay calm and treat the most serious problems first.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: What are the signs that someone might need CPR? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What are the signs that someone might need CPR?
  • Answer: Unresponsive, not breathing or gasping, no pulse.
  • A person may need CPR when they are completely unresponsive and do not react to
  • calling or tapping. They may not be breathing at all, or they may only gasp weakly,
  • which is not normal breathing. Their chest will not rise and fall normally. They may also
  • have no pulse or signs of circulation. In such situations, the person’s heart and breathing
  • have stopped, and CPR must be started immediately to keep blood and oxygen flowing
  • until medical help arrives.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Explain the steps to control bleeding in a first aid situation? (U) CO 4
questions.solution_html:
• Controlling bleeding is a crucial first -aid skill that can save lives. Before assisting, ensure the
  • scene is safe to avoid putting yourself at risk (e.g., sharp objects, traffic). Protecting yourself
  • prevents further harm or contamination. Do not remove anything is embedded in a wound. Apply
  • direct pressure to the wound with your fingers or the palm of your hand over a sterile wound
  • dressing to control the bleeding. Direct pressure helps compress blood vessels and reduces blood
  • flow, helps clotting. Raise t he injured body part above heart level. Once bleeding slows, secure
  • the dressing in place with a bandage. If bleeding soaks through, don’t remove the dressing, add
  • another layer. Severe blood loss can cause shock, which is life -threatening Look for symptoms
  • like pale, clammy skin, rapid breathing, or confusion. Lay the person down, keep them warm,
  • and raise their legs if no injury prevents it.

questions.question: Explain the concept of high-quality CPR and its components. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the concept of high‑quality CPR and its components.
  • Answer: 100 –120 compressions/min, proper depth, full recoil, minimal interruptions,
  • good ventilation.
  • High-quality CPR means giving chest compressions and breaths in the most effective
  • way to increase the person’s chance of survival. It includes pushing hard and fast at a rate
  • of 100–120 compressions per minute and pressing deep enough to help blood flow. The
  • chest should be allowed to come back fully after each compression. There should be very
  • few interruptions, and breaths should be given gently so the chest rises without over -
  • ventilating. Using an AED as soon as possible is also part of good CPR practice. All
  • these components together help maintain the flow of oxygen to the heart and brain.

questions.question: Describe the steps involved in providing first aid to a person with shock? / [CO5] [3x5 = 15]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the steps involved in providing first aid to a person with shock.
  • Answer: Lay them down, elevate legs, keep warm, control bleeding, monitor breathing,
  • and call emergency help.
  • When giving first aid for shock, the first aider should quickly call for medical help and
  • keep the person lying down. The legs can be raised slightly to improve blood flow to vital
  • organs, unless there is a suspected injury that prevents it. The person should be kept
  • warm using a blanket to prevent further heat loss. Any visib le bleeding must be
  • controlled immediately by applying pressure. The first aider should stay calm, reassure
  • the person, and monitor their breathing and response. Nothing should be given to eat or
  • drink, and the person must not be moved unnecessarily. These steps help maintain
  • circulation and prevent the condition from getting worse.
